description: The People's Budget, the Lords crisis, the Parliament Act 1911 and the rise of Labour.
content_html:
The Liberal Landslide of 1906

The general election of January 1906 transformed British politics. The Conservatives, associated with the Boer War and with Joseph Chamberlain’s controversial tariff reform proposals, suffered a crushing defeat. The Liberals won 397 seats and formed a majority government. Their victory was reinforced by an informal pact with the newly formed Labour Representation Committee, which won 29 seats and became the Labour Party.

The new Liberal government faced immense social and political challenges. Reports by Charles Booth and Seebohm Rowntree had revealed that roughly one-third of the population lived in poverty. At the same time, the House of Lords remained dominated by Conservative peers who were ready to reject legislation they disliked. The collision between Liberal ambition, social need and aristocratic obstruction defined the decade before the First World War.

Key Fact

The Liberals won 397 seats in January 1906, the largest majority in British history to that point. The Labour Party was formally established the same year, winning 29 seats.

The People’s Budget, 1909

The constitutional crisis began with the budget of April 1909, introduced by Chancellor David Lloyd George. He needed to raise money to pay for both the new welfare reforms (old age pensions had come into force in 1908) and an expensive naval arms race with Germany. Lloyd George proposed new taxes targeting the wealthy: a super-tax on high incomes, increased death duties, a 20 per cent tax on land value increases (the “land tax”), and increased income tax.

Lloyd George deliberately presented the budget as a class confrontation. He gave speeches attacking hereditary landowners, famously asking: “A fully equipped duke costs as much to keep up as two Dreadnoughts; and dukes are just as great a terror, and they last longer.” This rhetoric united Liberal and Labour support behind the budget but inflamed Conservative and aristocratic opposition. When the Commons passed the budget in November 1909, the House of Lords rejected it by 350 votes to 75 — breaking the constitutional convention that the Lords did not block money bills.

Prime Minister Asquith called two general elections in 1910 — in January and December — to seek a mandate to curb the Lords’ power. Both elections returned a hung Parliament: the Liberals and Labour depended on the votes of Irish Nationalist MPs, who supported reform in exchange for a promise of Irish Home Rule. King George V’s agreement (under pressure) to create up to 500 new Liberal peers — which would have swamped the Conservative majority in the Lords — forced the Lords to capitulate. Many Conservative peers chose to abstain rather than face dilution; the Parliament Bill passed in August 1911.

The Parliament Act, 1911

The Parliament Act 1911 was a landmark constitutional reform. It established that:

  • The House of Lords could not reject or amend money bills (the Speaker of the Commons would certify what counted as a money bill).
  • The Lords could delay other legislation by up to two years, but could not block it permanently.
  • General elections would be held every five years, not seven (reducing the parliament term from seven years).

The Act fundamentally shifted the balance of power between the elected Commons and the unelected Lords. It also made it possible for the Liberals to pass controversial legislation — including Home Rule for Ireland and Welsh Church Disestablishment — even against Lords opposition, since the Lords could only delay, not defeat, such bills.

Key Fact

The Parliament Act 1911 removed the Lords’ power to block money bills entirely and limited their power over other legislation to a two-year delay. It was the most significant restriction of Lords power since the English Civil War.

The Rise of Trade Unions and Labour

The period 1900–1914 saw the trade union movement grow dramatically. Membership rose from around 2 million in 1900 to over 4 million by 1914. The unions faced a serious legal challenge when the Taff Vale case of 1901 established that unions could be sued for losses caused by strikes, exposing union funds to ruinous claims. This pushed the trade union movement firmly into politics: it was a major reason why unions funded Labour candidates in 1906.

The Liberal government reversed the Taff Vale judgement with the Trade Disputes Act 1906, which restored trade union immunity from damages claims. However, a second legal threat came with the Osborne judgement of 1909, which ruled that trade unions could not use their funds to pay MPs’ salaries or support political parties. Since Labour MPs depended on union wages (no MPs were paid from public funds until 1911), this threatened Labour’s existence. The payment of MPs was introduced in 1911, and the Trade Union Act 1913 restored the right of unions to support political parties.

Keir Hardie was the most prominent early figure of the Labour movement. A former coal miner from Scotland, he was elected to Parliament in 1892 as one of the first working-class MPs and consistently argued that only a party independent of the Liberal Party could truly represent workers’ interests. He co-founded the Independent Labour Party in 1893 and was a key figure in creating the Labour Representation Committee in 1900, which became the Labour Party in 1906. Hardie opposed the Boer War and later campaigned against Britain’s entry into the First World War.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain a Cause’ questions about the Lords crisis, move beyond simply saying Lloyd George’s budget was rejected. Explain why the budget provoked such opposition (land taxes, class politics, Lloyd George’s rhetoric) and trace the chain from cause to effect (Lords reject budget → elections → threat of new peers → Parliament Act). For ‘Evaluate an Interpretation’ 12-mark questions, you must agree and disagree using precise contextual knowledge before giving a judgement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Liberal landslide of 1906 created the political conditions for a decade of reform. Lloyd George’s People’s Budget of 1909 deliberately targeted the wealthy and triggered the Lords crisis.
  • The Parliament Act 1911 removed the Lords’ veto over money bills and limited their power over other legislation to a two-year delay — a fundamental shift in constitutional power.
  • The Labour Party emerged from the trade union movement and survived legal threats (Taff Vale, Osborne) largely through Liberal legislation; by 1914 it was an established force with over 40 MPs.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of David Lloyd George's People's Budget of 1909.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed point. Example: The budget introduced a new super-tax on high incomes (1), targeting wealthy landowners and top earners to pay for welfare reforms and naval rearmament (1). Mastering: accurate feature with supporting detail. Developing: feature stated but undeveloped.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Parliament Act of 1911.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature examples: Lords could not block money bills; Lords could only delay other legislation by two years; maximum term of a parliament reduced to five years. Mastering: two precise features with accurate supporting detail. Developing: features without adequate development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the House of Lords rejected the People's Budget in 1909.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Developed explanation with accurate contextual knowledge. E.g. the budget proposed land-value taxes that would directly hit aristocratic landowners who dominated the Lords; Lloyd George's provocative language framing the budget as a class war inflamed opposition; Conservative peers saw the budget as an attack on the propertied classes and felt justified in using their blocking power. Secure (3–4): clear cause with some development. Developing (1–2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Taff Vale case of 1901 for the Labour Party.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Consequence developed with supporting knowledge. The ruling that unions could be sued for strike losses threatened union funds; this pushed trade unions to fund independent Labour candidates in 1906 to obtain parliamentary protection; the Liberal government responded with the Trade Disputes Act 1906 restoring union immunity, but the episode had cemented the union–Labour alliance. Secure (3–4): clear consequence with some development. Developing (1–2): simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Parliament Act 1911 for British democracy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): Significance at the time AND over time. At the time: removed Lords’ absolute veto, enabling Liberal welfare and constitutional reforms to pass; established elected Commons’ supremacy. Over time: set the precedent for later Lords reform (1949 Parliament Act); made the Lords a revising rather than blocking chamber; foundation of modern constitutional balance. Secure (5–6): both dimensions, some development of each. Developing (3–4): one dimension only. Emerging (1–2): simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: 'The Lords crisis of 1909–1911 was caused mainly by Lloyd George's confrontational style.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Agrees and disagrees, substantiated, reaches an overall judgement. Agree: Lloyd George’s rhetoric, 'fully equipped duke' speeches, land taxes directly targeting Lords’ wealth provoked an avoidable confrontation. Disagree: structural causes were deeper — Lords had blocked Liberal bills before 1909; the Conservatives lost two elections and still used the Lords to obstruct; the constitutional convention barring Lords from blocking money bills already existed. Own-knowledge synthesis: Asquith’s plan to flood Lords with new peers was the mechanism that resolved it. Secure (7–9): reasoned argument both ways. Developing (4–6): limited development. Emerging (1–3): one-sided.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Liberal Party's landslide general election victory?
Who introduced the People's Budget in 1909?
flashcard_questions.a: David Lloyd George, Chancellor of the Exchequer.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Lords do with the People's Budget in November 1909?
flashcard_questions.a: Rejected it by 350 votes to 75, breaking convention on money bills.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Parliament Act 1911 do to the Lords' power over money bills?
flashcard_questions.a: Removed it entirely — the Lords could no longer block money bills.

flashcard_questions.q: How long could the Lords delay other legislation after the Parliament Act 1911?
What was the Taff Vale case of 1901?
flashcard_questions.a: A ruling that unions could be sued for losses caused by strikes, threatening union funds.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Act restored trade union immunity from damages claims after the Taff Vale case?
What did the Osborne judgement of 1909 rule?
flashcard_questions.a: That trade unions could not use their funds to pay MPs or support political parties.

flashcard_questions.q: When were MPs first paid a salary from public funds?

flashcard_questions.a: A Scottish miner and MP, co-founder of the Independent Labour Party and first Labour Party leader.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Labour Party formally established?
What did tariff reform propose, and why did it split the Conservative Party?
flashcard_questions.a: Taxes on imports to protect industry and empire; free traders opposed it as raising prices for consumers.

glossary_terms.definition: A policy of taxing imported goods to protect home industries and bind the empire, championed by Joseph Chamberlain and opposed by free traders.
The unelected upper chamber of Parliament, which retained the power to block legislation until the Parliament Act 1911 curtailed that power.
Liberal Chancellor of the Exchequer (1908–1915) and chief architect of the People's Budget (1909) and the campaign against the Lords.
The Act that stripped the House of Lords of the power to block money bills and limited its veto on other legislation to two years.
Scottish miner and politician (1856–1915), co-founder of the Independent Labour Party and first leader of the Labour Party in Parliament.
